World.title: Packed New Plymouth hall hears arguments against Taranaki LNG facility
World.content:
Photo: RNZ / Robin Martin

About 100 people have packed into the St Mary's Peace Hall in New Plymouth to hear from critics of a proposal for a liquified natural gas import facility at Port Taranaki.

The government says with gas supply dwindling, LNG will shore up electricity supply during dry years, keep the lights on and prevent businesses closing. Opponents believe it locks New Zealand into a fossil-fuelled future and is hazardous.

Extra seats had to be rolled out at the "Why importing LNG is a bad idea" event, hosted by Climate Justice Taranaki, Taranaki Energy Watch and Community Energy Taranaki.

Photo: RNZ / Robin Martin

Retired energy systems analyst Steve Goldthorpe told the crowd LNG imports were not necessary.

"It's difficult and expensive and managing the hazards is a major difficulty and it's simply the wrong technology for New Zealand. It will lock us into importing expensive gas when we don't really need it for power generation."

He said alternatives already existed.

"Big grid-scale batteries to do the daily ups and downs and we've always had the ability to up and down the flow through some of the hydro turbines.

"And then for the long-term storage, the power companies are getting together to have a nice big stockpile of coal outside Huntly power station ready to do the dry-year job."

Goldthorpe said the coal could eventually be replaced by emissions-free wood chip technologies, which would also help remove forestry slash from New Zealand's hillsides.

Photo: RNZ / Robin Martin

Community Energy Taranaki's Steve Francis thought renewables was the way to go.

"I mean we're all about a positive future and saying yes to electrification, saying yes to renewables, and so based on what we're seeing in the market at the moment the tipping point for solar [has been reached].

"Like solar is the cheapest form of energy now and with increased electrification we just don't see any need for LNG."

Francis wanted to see cheap loans made available for residential solar.

"Solar uptake in New Zealand is something like 3 percent of residential. In Australia it's 40 percent so we've got enormous potential to electrify things, to get solar panels on our roofs. And it's good for the cost of living, good for greenhouse gas emissions, it's even good for local employment."

Energy Minister responds

In a statement, Energy Minister Simeon Brown said New Zealand was fortunate that 88 percent of electricity already came from renewable resources - mostly hydro but also wind, geothermal and solar.

"However, from time to time, most recently just two years ago, the country experiences a 'dry year' when lakes are low, the wind isn't blowing, the sun isn't shining and there is insufficient generation to meet peak demand - often in the evenings during winter. These conditions can continue for weeks."

Photo: RNZ / Mark Papalii

Brown said New Zealand had relied on burning coal and gas for back-up, or "firming", in these circumstances.

"As gas supplies dwindle, LNG is a potential back-up for generating electricity to keep the lights on for all New Zealanders and to prevent manufacturing shutting down, thereby threatening jobs and incomes.

"It's an insurance policy so that all users can have confidence in a reliable electricity supply."

Brown said the government totally supported renewables and had fast-tracked several renewable electricity generation projects that were now in the pipeline.

"But unlike the previous government that banned oil and gas exploration, we are not so one-eyed that we will let the lights go out rather than ensure there is back-up electricity generation for New Zealanders when it's needed. LNG can provide that."

Photo: RNZ / Robin Martin

Energy Watch Taranaki's Sarah Roberts worried about the safety of a LNG terminal at Port Taranaki.

"Basically it's the wrong place. No one is looking at the location. Why do we have to put it right next to thousands of people's homes, schools - you know, communities that live and play at the beach?

"And here we are wanting to put a major industry - bigger than what we've ever had before - right in the middle of it."

She said in a worse-case scenario, fatalities could be expected over a wide area from an explosion at a facility at Port Taranaki.

Brown said the government was going through a procurement process and no final decisions had been made.

"But LNG is a proven and safe energy option. No health and safety standards would be compromised to allow for LNG firming capacity."

Most meeting-goers were against the proposal.

Alex thought it was a no-brainer.

"I don't think it's a good idea. I think the idea of tying us to a carbon future when we have all the evidence we need on climate change is absolutely ridiculous."

Oil and gas worker Steve was not convinced either.

"I don't think it's right for Taranaki and I don't think it's right for the port. It's a lot of money to invest. I'd like to see more in renewables."

For Chrissie Ryeburn, it was personal.

"I'm still concerned because we are in the blast zone but also all of the schools which are so close to that blast zone, which is about seven."

The government was aiming to finalise a location for an LNG import terminal and contract a preferred provider by the middle of this year.

If the procurement process was successful, the facility could be operational in 2027.

World.title: Ministry for the Environment officially scrapped in Parliament vote
World.content:
Photo: RNZ / REECE BAKER

The Ministry for the Environment has been scrapped, with legislation bringing the 40-year-old ministry to an end passing in Parliament on Wednesday night.

Its demise makes way for the creation of the new Ministry for Cities, Environment, Regions and Transport (MCERT).

Environment Minister Nicola Grigg says environmental responsibilities will continue seamlessly under the new arrangements.

"The Bill formally transfers the Ministry for the Environment's statutory functions under the Environment Act to the Secretary for the Environment," she said.

MCERT's chief executive would carry out the responsibilities of the Secretary for the Environment, Grigg said.

"Environmental functions remain central to the work of the new department. Integrating these portfolios will support more practical and joined-up decision-making that both protects the environment and supports economic growth."

The Green Party condemned the move, saying it cemented the coalition as the most anti-environment government in New Zealand's history.

Green Party environment spokesperson Lan Pham said none of the coalition partners campaigned on the change.

"New Zealanders of all political stripes care about the environment, swim in rivers, lakes, and at the beach, and fish for kai. They know that nature is the backbone of our economy. They did not ask for this," she said.

"At a time when all our environmental outcomes across freshwater, air, biodiversity and oceans are going backwards, climate change is flooding communities week after week, costing billions of dollars, lives, and livelihoods, this Government's response is to dismantle the ministry responsible for environmental protection," Pham said.

World.title: How the 'supereruption' that transformed NZ happened
World.content:
By Anna Miller of

Photo: Supplied / Katherine Holt, CC BY-NC-ND

Some 350,000 years ago, the centre of New Zealand's North Island appeared much different than the mountainous, scrub-covered landscape it is today.

Amid a glacial period, temperatures were colder and conditions harsher. Vast beech and podocarp forests blanketed the region, providing habitat for abundant native birdlife.

It was against this tranquil backdrop that the one of the Earth's most explosive eruptions violently unfolded, releasing enough material to carpet much of the country.

Now, colleagues and I have pieced together traces left by the event to provide an unprecedented picture of how it happened - while shedding important new light on the mechanics of those rare cataclysms that are known as supereruptions.

Reconstructing a supereruption

The Whakamaru supereruption was one of the largest ever recorded on Earth - and the greatest produced by New Zealand's famous Taupō Volcanic Zone.

Stretching from Whakaari/White Island to Ruapehu, this dynamic area is the product of two powerful geological processes: the Pacific Plate sinking beneath the Australian Plate, and the central North Island simultaneously being pulled apart.

It is home to numerous volcanic features today, from geothermal fields, with bubbling hot springs and mud pools, to caldera systems and active stratovolcanoes.

Throughout its 2-million-year history, the zone has experienced four known events of such immense scale that they are formally classified as supereruptions - or those that would score a maximum 8 on the Volcanic Explosivity Index.

Only a few dozen have ever been recorded worldwide - the most recent being the Ōruanui eruption that helped create Lake Taupō around 25,300 years ago.

For volcanologists, they pose some of the field's greatest mysteries: how can so much magma build up below the surface, and then erupt all at once? And what happens to the surrounding landscapes?

To help answer these questions, we turn to preserved volcanic deposits that can be used to reconstruct the processes that play out during these rare events.

Two signature products of supereruptions are "flow" deposits - hot, dangerous masses of rock and gas that travel along the ground - and "fall" deposits, typically mixtures of crystals and volcanic glass that fall from the air.

The challenge for volcanologists is that typically only fragments of these deposits are preserved - and they are often scattered across great distances.

In the Whakamaru supereruption, massive pyroclastic flows left behind thick layers of dense volcanic rock across the Whakamaru and King Country regions. Ash and pumice spread much farther, blanketing much of the North Island and parts of the Pacific Ocean.

One of the first steps in our study was to build a database of these deposits by matching the unique chemical signature of volcanic glass produced during the eruption.

Photo: Supplied / Anna Miller

This process is similar to forensic science at a crime scene: fingerprints may suggest a suspect, but DNA evidence can confirm the match. In volcanology, deposits can offer clues as to how they got there, but it is their chemical composition which provides the definitive link.

Using this approach, we analysed more than 30 sites around New Zealand and the south Pacific Ocean. All were found to have come from the Whakamaru supereruption.

With these correlated, we were then able to reconstruct this extraordinary episode.

How the supereruption unfolded

At the beginning of the eruption, a large lake likely lay within the central North Island, much like Lake Taupō today.

When the magma reached the surface, it erupted directly into this lake, triggering extremely violent interactions between magma and water, which drove the earliest phase of the eruption.

Photo: Supplied / Anna Miller CC BY-NC-ND

It appears this first phase was driven by the evacuation of a singular magma body.

As the eruption progressed, the lake was gradually destroyed and infilled. Eventually, the system transitioned into a much drier style of volcanism.

At the same time, the eruption evolved into a far larger and more complex event beneath the surface. Instead of being fed by one magma chamber, it appears to have triggered a cascading sequence involving at least five separate magma bodies erupting at once.

The amount of ash generated by the eruption is staggering.

Most of the North Island - and even far-away Chatham Island - would have been carpeted in around 30cm or more of material. Areas closer to the eruption were left buried under as much as 4.5m of ash.

Photo: Supplied / Anna Miller CC BY-NC-ND

Hot, dense pyroclastic flows also swept across the landscape, leaving deposits up to hundreds of metres thick closer to the eruption source.

Altogether, we estimate the eruption released around 2,300 cubic kilometres of volcanic material - enough to bury the entirety of New Zealand beneath roughly nine metres of debris if spread evenly from Cape Reinga to Invercargill.

Photo: Supplied / Anna Miller CC BY-NC-ND

Today, the Taupō Volcanic Zone remains one of the most active and powerful volcanic systems on Earth.

Although supereruptions like Whakamaru are rare, Taupō volcano has produced many smaller yet still devastating eruptions throughout its history, all of which would have had major impacts on both New Zealand and the wider world.

Understanding how these types of volcanoes operate is essential, both in preparing for future eruptions and for understanding how past events may have transformed the landscape we see today.

*The author acknowledges the contributions of Simon Baker and Colin Wilson to this research.

*Anna Millar is a PhD Candidate, School of Geography, Environment and Earth Sciences, Te Herenga Waka - Victoria University of Wellingtona

This story was first published by The Conversation

World.title: Air New Zealand cuts another blow to regions, airport industry group says
World.content:
Photo: AFP

An airport industry group says further cuts to Air New Zealand's schedule is another blow for the regions.

The national carrier was notifying customers of further schedule changes as the jet fuel crisis bites.

Earlier this month, Air New Zealand announced it was cutting five percent of its flights, mostly on regional routes.

New Zealand Airports Association chief executive Billie Moore told Checkpoint regional connectivity had already been declining for several years.

"It's not unexpected, but yeah, it is another blow," she said.

"The issue isn't necessarily the call to shave roots at this point with the fuel price, it's the base on which that shaving is happening.

"We've been in decline for many years now and for regional [Q300 turboprop plane] capacity, if we compare to 2019, the decline is closer to 27 percent. So quite a chunk of connectivity coming out of the market over that period of time, which really does hurt."

Further schedule cuts would continue to erode the regional network, which had already been impacted by an ageing fleet of aircrafts.

Air New Zealand said less than two percent of customers travelling during this time will be affected, with the "vast majority" of those impacted still able to travel on the same day.

Moore said for regional flights there had been a capacity decline of about 10 percent in 12 months.

"We do see a heavier impact for those routes because they are smaller. When you take a flight out, the proportion impact is higher."

Although Air New Zealand had a significant role to play when it came to the economic well-being of the regions, criticism of the airline for optimising its commercial situation during a fuel crisis was misplaced.

"Overall, our challenge is how can we work together to create a situation where [Air New Zealand] will invest in the regions and add capacity over time," Moore said.

Moore said despite assurances from the national carrier, regional airports were feeling anxious over the prospect cuts could become permanent.

"There will be further engagement between Air New Zealand and the regions coming up. I hope it is positive," she said.

"And I know the sentiment from everybody is that we want the airline to be profitable."

World.title: Gulf Harbour body trial: accused seeks return of deported women
World.content:
Photo: RNZ / Marika Khabazi

The leader of a religious group who is one of four people accused of the kidnapping and manslaughter of Shulai Wang has asked an immigration officer in court whether they can help to bring to the trial other Chinese women who had lived in his home and who were deported.

Kaixiao Liu, his wife Lanyue Xiao and his parents Xiuyun Li and Jingui Liu have each denied the kidnapping and manslaughter of Wang.

They are all self-represented in the trial, accompanied by standby lawyers.

Wang's body, wrapped in layers of rubbish bags, was found by a fisherman in the waters of Auckland's Gulf Harbour on 12 March, 2024, eight months after she entered the country.

The Crown said Wang, aged 70, was one of six women who came to New Zealand to seek religious instructions from Kaixiao Liu and lived "in servitude" to Liu's family in their home in Orewa and called Liu "the lord".

The Crown earlier said the other women refused to talk to police, and immigration officers told the court that police did not oppose the deportation as the women were no longer needed for the investigation.

It argued that Wang was starved and punished for disobeying the rules of the group and subsequently bound in tape after a failed escape attempt.

On Wednesday, the jury heard that the five other women in the house, also referred to by the group as the 'Ark', had overstayed their visas when they were discovered by police during a search warrant on the defendants' home on Harvest Avenue in July 2024.

Crown witness and immigration officer Alexander Ballerau told the jury that the five women were all Chinese citizens and were all unlawfully in New Zealand at the time.

Two of the women's last date of arrival in New Zealand was January 2020. The other three arrived in 2023.

Ballerau also said that the five women did not speak during their individual interviews with immigration officers and neither did they engage with Mandarin interpreters.

He said three of the women "simply smiled" throughout the interview.

Earlier, the court heard from Crown Prosecutor Emma Kerr that apart from initial comments, the five women refused to engage with police.

Ballerau said the women were all deported in August 2024.

Asked by Kerr if police were content with the deportation and that the women were no longer needed for the investigation, Ballerau said yes.

During Kaixiao Liu's cross-examination of another immigration officer, Mohammed Arour, he asked if the officer had any way to "help those ladies come to the trial, because they want to", adding that it was for "open justice" and the "search of truth".

He was interrupted by Justice Downs who told him he could not assume in his questions what other people were thinking, and he was urged to rephrase his question.

Arour said the Immigration Minister could over-ride the five-year prohibition that prevented a deported person from re-entering, and that could be applied for through an immigration adviser or lawyer.

Liu asked if it could be done within three weeks, to which Arour said he could not answer that.

Liu's wife Xiao cross-examined Ballerau on the deportation of the five women.

She asked if they were told about their right to appeal the order, to which Ballerau said that right expired 42 days after the expiry of their visa and they had all overstayed beyond that time limit.

Xiao's standby lawyer Quentin Duff asked Ballerau if overstayers involved in criminal proceedings would be allowed to stay.

Ballerau said that was correct and that it also applied to witnesses.

Duff asked if the decision to deport the women was discussed with police investigating Wang's death.

Ballerau said immigration, not police, made deportation decisions. "However, when police advise they're no longer of interest, we are free to proceed with our processes", he said.

The trial continues.

World.title: Cooks dengue-free, but cases still being reported in other areas of the Pacific
World.content:
Photo: 123RF

The Cook Islands is now dengue fever free, but other regions of the Pacific are still seeing cases.

Cases of dengue fever in Tonga have reached 66.

As of Monday, 25 May, two cases were hospitalised - one at Princess Fusipala Hospital in Ha'apai and one at Niu'eiki Hospital in 'Eua.

No deaths have been reported in Tonga's current outbreak.

Cases are also being reported this month in New Caledonia and Samoa, and in Futuna.

In the Cooks, 1251 cases were reported in the last outbreak, one of whom died.

Secretary for Health Bob Williams told Cook Islands News that the last positive case was recorded on 28 April.

Sunday marked 26 days since that case.

Williams said the 26-day period represents just over two incubation periods with no reported case, which meets the international standard to declare the outbreak over.

Liana Scott, president of the Cook Islands Tourism Industry Council, said the swift response played an important role in containing the situation, but warned that the dengue-free declaration "does not mean that we should become complacent".

"Businesses and households should be encouraged to maintain grounds and potential [mosquito] breeding areas," she said.

Meanwhile, larvae from a type of exotic mosquito that can carry diseases were found in downtown Auckland nearly two months ago.

New Zealand's National Public Health Service had launched a surveillance and interception programme after the discovery of the aedes aegypti larvae in a trap near Queens wharf.

The mosquito breed could carry diseases including dengue fever, yellow fever, zika virus and chikungunya virus.

The service said exotic species were occasionally found at ports and airports.

It said the larvae was not considered a public health or biosecurity threat at the time because there was no indication they had become established.

World.title: Maroons let 20-0 lead slip in Origin I after Kalyn Ponga sent off late
World.content:
James Tedesco has scored a spectacular try with 90 seconds left in State of Origin I to cap off a stunning comeback to win State of Origin I 22-20 at a sodden Stadium Australia.

An electric Queensland outfit shot out to a 20-0 lead after 20 minutes of the series opener in Sydney, before spending an hour desperately trying to cling on.

That task was made harder when superstar fullback Kalyn Ponga was sent off for a shoulder charge on a flying Tolu Koula after 57 minutes.

Loading Instagram content

Cameron Munster and Ponga insisted that it was the fullback's head, not his shoulder, that hit Koula high.

But Ashley Klein would not be moved, noting Ponga's shoulder-charge action before making the Newcastle fullback the seventh man to be sent off in an Origin match, although not everyone agreed.

"I'm still in shock about the Kalyn Ponga decision," Queensland legend Darren Lockyer said on Channel Nine after the game.

Kalyn Ponga had played a sensational game until his blunder. (Getty Images: Darrian Traynor)

"Credit to New South Wales, but there will be plenty of people north of the border who will struggle to accept that decision."

The score at that stage was 20-6 for Queensland but the send off completely changed the complexion of the contest.

Debutant Ethan Strange and halfback Nathan Cleary scored on 62 and 71 minutes, as the Maroons' defence scrambled in the wet.

They repelled the Blues until the final moments, when Cleary's bomb landed a metre in front of the tryline and Tedesco outleapt Hamiso Tabuai-Fidow, pinched the ball, juggled and regathered on the way to grounding.

James Tedesco scored a miracle try in the final 90 seconds to win the game for the Blues. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer)

"That was unreal, a bit surreal to be honest," Tedesco, the reigning Dally M medallist who was playing his first Origin match since Game I of 2024.

"We dug deep, we knew we'd get some opportunities.

"We made too many errors [in the first half] … we made it hard for ourselves.

"We had plenty of opportunities and I'm just glad I came up with something."

Cleary potted the extras from just next to the posts and NSW took a 1-0 series lead before the series heads to Melbourne for Game II in three weeks' time.

The Blues will celebrate tonight, but will be left wondering how Queensland got such a jump on them in the opening exchanges.

Uncharacteristic errors from Brian To'o and Stephen Crichton didn't help the Blues, but the Maroons were utterly irresistible for the first half hour of the game.

Tom Flegler was swarmed by his teammates after scoring a try in his return to the Origin arena. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer)

Robert Toia, Thomas Flegler and Hamiso Tabuai-Fidow all scored in the opening 16 minutes of the match, with Sam Walker playing brilliantly on debut, kicking four goals from four.

But the Blues scored off their very first foray into the Maroons end, Hudson Young scoring off a magical kick by Nathan Cleary, who was later awarded player of the match honours.

They Blues could have had a second before the break only for Cameron Murray to be penalised for a foul before grounding in the in-goal.

The game evolved into an arm wrestle early in the second half, before Ponga's crucial collision, which resulted in Koula being subbed out of the game with a concussion and Ponga fined 23 per cent of his match fee.

Look back on how all the action unfolded in our live blog.

Live updates State of Origin Game I S By Simon Smale Collapse all posts off Sort Sort posts Latest Select an option New: Filters Choose what information you see below by using filters Filter Posts All 124 Key Events 19 Tries 7 Goals 1 Comments 12 All filters Time to say goodbye S By Simon Smale (Getty Images) Well, a stunning victory for the Blues, as dramatic as it could possibly be, with the people's champion James Tedesco scoring the winner on his return to the Origin stage. Genuinely couldn't happen to a nicer guy. As far as Queensland will be concerned, that was one that got away. To be 20-0 up and still lose the game, no matter the circumstances, is a failure and puts the defending champions on the back foot heading to the MCG next month. Was the Ponga send off correct? I think it depends on who you are talking to. The fact is that Tolu Koula was unable to resume the match after the incident due to the contact. There is also, from the alternative side, that Ashley Klein overruled the Bunker official who told him the incident did not meet the threshold for a send off. That conversation will rumble on and on. But, for now, our conversation is over. Thanks so much for being with us on a soggy night in capitals either side of the border. Until we meet again, at the MCG on June 17. 'The Blues don't win that game unless Ponga gets sent off': Paul Gallen S By Simon Smale Paul Gallen is speaking on Channel Nine at the moment. He is pretty adamant that the Blues were the second best team on the ground throughout the opening exchanges. He says that the Blues may even need to make a couple of changes ahead of the second game. "The Blues don't win that game unless Ponga gets sent off," Ponga says. "I think they need to keep a lid on it and pick a team that can win Game II because you do not want to go up to Queensland for a decider." Murray credits Blues pressure S By Simon Smale Cameron Murray is speaking now to Channel Nine. He still looks to be in a bit of shock about how the game was turned around so late. He is asked about what the Blues did well when the Maroons were down to 12 men, and he says that it was basically just their pressure. "We probably just did a great job with building pressure," Murray says. "We just put a bit more fatigue in their defensive line." They sure did - the Blues dominated late on, at one stage earning seven sets in a row against the Maroons increasingly desperate defence. Daley won't be drawn on the Ponga decision J By Jon Healy The NSW coach is asked about Kalyn Ponga being sent off the field. "I'd rather not say," he says. I'll leave it to you to decipher that. Does he want to avoid being panned for kicking a bloke when he's down or did he disagree with the call? I think more likely the former, but he's not given us much to go off. Captain Isaah Yeo says he thinks it was a send-off, but admits he's hardly an impartial observer. "Bias says I think it's a send off. We've been on that side of it as well. I don't know." Daley says this is nothing new. "If you look through Origin history there's always been moment and there's always been wins like that; you take 'em." Slater's pride J By Jon Healy Slater pretty much always talks about being proud of his team, but you can tell there's a little more feeling behind it tonight. "We've gotta take some positives out of what we did tonight, and there were a lot. "It's natural to feel heartbroken and disappointed but we won't be throwing the baby out with the bath water." The coach is asked what he's most proud of. "The heart and spirit they fought with. "Twenty-three minutes in a State of Origin game with 12 men, they fought hard. You could see they were just holding on in stages. "One moment at the end of the game it could be a different story, but it's not. "I'm sure all Queenslanders are proud of their footy team right now." 'I suggest you ask someone else': Gould refuses to talk about send off S By Simon Smale The Channel Nine team are talking about the send off. There are mixed feelings. "We could hear the thump [sideline]," Darren Lockyer says. "I looks sickening from a distance. "And I think Ashley Klein always had this [the send off] in his mind. "The Bunker said it should be 10 minutes ... but Ashley Klein didn't have a bar of it." Brad Fittler is more accepting of the call. "As the defender, you have responsibility ... you have to be on the down side," Fittler says. "That's why he was sent off." As for what Gus Gould thinks? He pleads the fifth. "I suggest you ask someone else, not me," Gus Gould says. Interesting. "He's probably thinking he's cost the team the game," Lockyer says. "There will be a lot of people in the changing room at the moment, who will be perplexed at how that happened." Billy Slater has no problems with Kalyn Ponga send-off J By Jon Healy Queensland coach Billy Slater says the decision to send Kalyn Ponga off "is what it is". "I haven't got any problems with it. "I'm not gonna make any noise about it. They're the breaks." He says Ponga "obviously feels like he let his team down". Captain Cameron Munster says he felt like the speed of the incident and the fact Ponga tried to get low with Tolu Koula, plus the head-to-head contact, might have meant it was only a sin-bin. "I thought it might have been head on head but the ref and the bunker saw it differently. Those are the rules. Ref's gotta make a split decision." Strange 'sparked' the Blues: Johns S By Simon Smale Andrew Johns says Ethan Strange "sparked" the Blues. "You're looking at a guy who may play 30 Origins," he says. "After KP got sent off and the field opened up, he was "devastating Cameron Smith agrees. "I agree," he says.

"It was a wonderful debut." Darren Lockyer 'in shock' over Ponga send off S By Simon Smale Here is Queensland legend Darren Lockyer. He is very, very unhappy. "I'm still in shock about the Kalyn Ponga decision," he says. "Credit to New South Wales, but there will be plenty of people north of the border who will struggle to accept that decision." Young 'proud' of Strange S By Simon Smale Hudson Young is being interviewed now on Nine. "I am so proud of Ethan," he says. :First time he stepped on the field you knew he would be an Origin player, and he stepped up tonight." Gould: 'The first 25 minutes was everything I feared' S By Simon Smale "The first 25 minutes was everything I feared," says Gus Gould on Nine. "They started the second half pretty positively. "There was some really magical individual moments. I don't want playing against 12 men to take away from what he [Nathan Cleary] did under very difficult conditions. 'Greatest' Origin comeback ever? S By Simon Smale How can the NSW origin win be called the greatest come back win, when NSW played against 10 men for the greater part of the 2nd half? Poor decision by the referee against the spirit of state of origin rugby, that may set a precedent for future origin games. Ridiculous call! - Victorian Dale Not sure you can call it the “greatest origin comeback” when it’s a home game and 13 vs 12…. - Lj The blues played terribly for a team that was a man up for a quarter of the game. When Ponga went off I was expecting a blow out - Josh So NSW can win an Origin! (Against 12) - Muzz 'A different level': Haumole Olakau'atu S By Simon Smale Haumole Olakau'atu is speaking to ABC Sport too. He could have won the game much earlier for the Blues only to drop the ball with a three-man overlap. "I should've caught that but as I bent over to catch the ball everything just locked up and that was my night," he says. "Bad pass or not you still gotta execute and it wasn't good enough from my end. "I'm just glad Tedesco did that. If it was anyone else I don't know whether they would've pulled it off. "All these talks about the speed of the game is next level and it was no joke. This … is a different level." 'They're a hard enough team to defend when you've got a full team': Capewell S By Simon Smale (@ABCSport) Kurt Capewell has been speaking to ABC Sport too. "Definitely disappointing. We set the game up well and to lose like that hurts, but that's footy," he says. "They're a hard enough team to defend when you've got a full team out there, let alone 12 men. "We'll learn from it." To quote Nathan Cleary, 'Origin, hey?' S By Simon Smale One of the great Origins. Not a perfect performance - probably one of the worst from a winning side in Origin - but holy hell what a ride. - Tom Tedesco: 'Nath ... was instrumental' S By Simon Smale (@ABCSport) Here's some more from James Tedesco, speaking to ABC Sport. "That was unreal, a bit surreal to be honest," he says. "We dug deep, we knew we'd get some opportunities. I bombed one earlier so I knew I had to make up for it. "We made too many errors [in the first half], it was very slippery, we made it hard for ourselves in the first half. "We had plenty of opportunities and I'm just glad I came up with something. "Nath put it on the spot. He was instrumental. Strangey was unreal." Sam Walker doesn't want to talk S By Simon Smale Sam Walker is speaking now. He doesn't want to but is being told he has to as the Channel Nine cameras pursue him across the Sydney turf. "It's a hard one to reflect on right now," he says. "Just disappointed I guess. "It's really special to be able to put the jersey on," he adds, looking anything but happy. 'It's just Origin, hey?' Nathan Cleary is man of the match S By Simon Smale Nathan Cleary sums up most of our thoughts about that game. "It's just Origin, hey?" he says. "Queensland got the jump on us, but a lot of the talk behind the line was really positive. "Obviously pretty disappointed with that first half, not much defensive resilience." Ethan Strange 'that was pretty special' S By Simon Smale Ethan Strange is speaking now. "That was pretty special that one," he says. "Playing with all these guys, they're legends of the game. "How about Nathan Cleary? "The way he manages the game is incredible." He says it was a blur of a match. He genuinely looks stunned to be out there still, living his dream. Show more posts
